scenarios.title: The Requirement That Wasn't
scenarios.behaviour: Recognizes and inquires when there is more to what the client is communicating
scenarios.blurb: Sign-off is on Friday, the spec says 'notify the customer', and nobody has asked what happens when the customer has no phone number.

brief.title: Two days to sign-off
brief.text: You are the BA on a refunds release. The spec line reads: 'When a refund is approved, notify the customer.' Ops has signed it. Tech has estimated it. Everyone is comfortable. You are not, and you cannot yet say why.

n1.prompt: Sign-off is Friday. What do you do with the discomfort?

choices.label: Let it go - it is one line and everyone has signed

consequence.title: Week three of production
consequence.text: Refunds approve fine. Then a customer with no mobile number on file gets nothing, complains to the regulator, and the ticket lands back on your desk with a severity tag on it.
consequence.lesson: A requirement everyone agrees on is not the same as a requirement everyone read the same way. Consensus hides ambiguity, it does not resolve it.

choices.label: Ask ops for a concrete case: a refund last week and exactly what the customer received

consequence.title: The example does the work
consequence.text: Ops pulls a real refund. Turns out 'notify' means SMS, and about one in nine customers has no mobile number. Nobody had decided what those customers get. It was never a disagreement - it was a blank.
consequence.lesson: Concrete cases surface gaps that abstract review never will. Ask what happened last Tuesday, not whether the requirement is clear.

choices.label: Send the spec round again asking everyone to re-read carefully

consequence.title: Three replies, all 'looks fine'
consequence.text: You get three thumbs-ups within the hour. Nobody read it again. The same line means SMS to ops, email to tech, and 'something automatic' to the sponsor, and the round trip cost you half a day.
consequence.lesson: Re-reading the same words produces the same interpretation. Change the question, not the number of reviewers.

n2.prompt: You have twenty minutes with ops. Which of these must be nailed down before Friday? Pick every one that matters.

options.label: Which channel counts as a notification
options.sub: SMS, email, in-app, or any of them

options.label: What happens when the chosen channel is unavailable for that customer
The wording of the notification message
Who owns the decision when the channel fails
Which font the message template uses

n2.successNote: Channel definition, the failure case, and the decision owner. Wording can be drafted later; it does not change the build.

criteria.label: Names the specific channel rather than 'notify'
criteria.coach: name the channel that actually fires - 'notify' is the word that let two teams build two different things, and replacing it with 'SMS' or 'email' is what closes the gap

criteria.label: Handles the case where the channel is not available
criteria.hint: the customer with no number on file
criteria.coach: say what happens to the customer with no number on file - that is the one in nine who got silence in production, and a requirement that ignores them is where the regulator complaint came from

criteria.label: States who or what decides the fallback
criteria.hint: who owns the call when it fails
criteria.coach: name who or what makes the call when the channel fails - unowned edge cases get decided quietly by whoever is on shift at 6pm, and you will not know it happened

n3.passNote: Channel, failure case, and owner. That line cannot be built two ways.
n3.speaker: The delivery lead:
n3.question: Fine - so write me the line. If two developers read it, I want them building the same thing.
n3.title: Write the line
n3.model: When a refund is approved, the system sends the customer an SMS to the mobile number on file. If no mobile number is on file, it sends the same notification by email instead. If neither is available, the refund is flagged to the ops queue and ops owns the decision on how the customer is told.
n3.modelExplain: This covers all three: it names the channel (SMS), handles the customer with no number (email fallback), and names the owner when both fail (ops). Edit it or submit it as it stands to see the grade.

good.title: The blank cell had nowhere to hide
good.moral: A good requirement is not one everyone agrees with. It is one nobody can misread.
good.verdict: You shipped on Friday, and the one-in-nine customer got a defined outcome instead of silence. The same line became the test case, which is why QA found nothing in week three.
revealed: You asked for a real refund instead of asking whether the spec was clear.
You separated what mattered before Friday from what could wait.
Channel, failure case and owner - all three in one line.

partial.title: Better, but still readable two ways
partial.moral: Ambiguity does not announce itself. It shows up as a support ticket in week three.
partial.verdict: Your line is sharper than the original, but a developer reading it still has a decision left to make - and they will make it quietly, at 6pm, without you.
revealed: You found the gap before sign-off, which is most of the job.
The written requirement left at least one thing to interpretation.
